219.title: quality of the evidence
219.content: In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. Also called: certainty of the evidence, confidence in the estimates of effect . The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout.

335.title: Public Health Workforce candidate
335.content: The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. Also called: Public health workforce . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 399.doc: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution
399.title: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution candidate
399.content: An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Also called: Health workforce education and training institution . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 411.title: Facility Type candidate
411.content: Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Also called: Facility type . 455.title: Remuneration candidate
455.content: Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 1054.title: Narrower
1054.content: . | In a national context an electronic health workforce registry can be considered the single authoritative source of health workforce information that can provide an accurate count of all health care personnel that either have worked or are currently working at national or sub-national levels, including in the private sector. | An electronic health workforce registry can be designed to authenticate and validate the existence of a health worker and provide essential details about that person. | In addition, a health workforce registry can ensure quality control, provide easy access to information on production, distribution and utilization of health personnel, and assist in budgeting, research development and advocacy. | A health workforce registry allows aggregation of health workforce data in several combinations and assists both national and sub-national ministries of health in producing essential indicator-based reports, as needed. | The health workforce registry is a central and essential component of a functional HRIS, as it contains important health worker attributes that can subsequently be linked to other relevant HRIS components. | Address policy and governance mechanism | Agree on a location to operate the registry | Assure privacy, security and confidentiality of health workforce data | Establish standardized reports | Number of health workforce by cadre, gender and facility | Number of expected retirements | Number of expected and completed renewals of license/credentials | Number of vacant positions by facility | Geographic distribution of total workforce by facility | Geographic distribution (by district) of male and female employees | Develop, test, and deploy a functional electronic health workforce registry | Establish appropriate access controls based on an agreed policies. | Design, test and deploy the electronic web-enabled registry based on national eHealth enterprise architecture. | Make available, at sub-national level, a replica of the registry with similar structure and functions, in order to collect and manage the minimum data set from authorized entities at sub-national-level. | Adhere to best practices in information systems design to assure accuracy, timeliness, completeness, reliability, privacy, security, and confidentiality of data and information systems and assets. | Illustration depicting a web-enabled electronic Health Workforce Registry with person-centric data entry screen and analytics display abilities | Based on national or sub-national eHealth enterprise information architecture, national and sub-national health authorities shall develop and deploy the registry. | The registry shall conform to best practices in information systems design in order to assure quality, accuracy, timeliness, completeness, reliability, privacy, security, and confidentiality of the data and information systems and assets. | Legally authorized users of the registry shall be required to have unique user names and passwords that will be provided by the national Steering Committee, on the approval of the highest health authority at national and sub-national levels. Level of access to the registry shall be determined by the national Steering Committee or its authorized agent. | The registry must be in compliance with all applicable national and sub-national laws related to privacy, security, and confidentiality of data. | The registry and its related physical assets shall be secured in accordance with applicable national and sub-national laws. | .

The handbook cites its reference 69 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Programme (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))A “coherent set or sequence of educational activities or communication designed and organized to achieve pre-determined learning objectives or accomplish a specific set of educational tasks over a sustained period” with the objective to improve health knowledge, skills and competencies applied to health and enable the training of new health workers. Health workforce education and training programmes will often have a numerus clausus that restricts the number of places for a given programme. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 91; PDF page 105). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 108 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Institution (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). Facility Type candidate Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 89; PDF page 103). 1285.content: Gender candidate Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Facility Type (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. Public Health Workforce candidate The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. 1295.title: Q
1295.content: quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. Remuneration candidate Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 1360.title: computable adjudication and agentic test harness
1360.content: Computable adjudication and agentic test harness. Also written: caaat-harness, ca&at-harness, .c&at-harness, c@t-harness . Please be introduced to a cat who acquires things, for whatever purpose — maybe somebody knows. Scope: the platform — skills, schemas, processes, the MCP server and the pipeline. Not what a folio IS (that is folio-assist-core), and not any folio’s own content, which lives in its own repository. | cat-harness, in the source Its own repository since the cutover; the in-tree copy is archived in folio-assistant’s fsh-guts. | RTFM — the cat-harness docs The agent–user interaction model, and what this harness is for. | The work plan is where you say what you are doing Claim a bean before you work, so a sibling session does not pick up the same item. | Make your first folio This repository is the platform; your content lives in its own. | Know which kind of thing you are writing A document is structured prose; a paper adds the block kinds whose assertion is a formal claim. | The documentation you will never read All of it. The honest expectation is that you arrive from a search engine when something breaks. | .

1361.title: What a folio is
1361.content: The knowledge graph is four sub-graphs, and a layer declares which of them it holds. Content is what somebody authors and a reader reads — this layer’s subject. Skills are the instructions an agent follows to do the work. Processes are the BPMN diagrams that say who does what, in which order, and where the gates are — they are executable, not illustrations. Tools are what an agent can call. Getting anything in is acquisition: unstructured and semi-structured sources arrive through uploads/ or through the conversation, and are ingested into library/. It is a step rather than a graph typology of its own — there is no fifth directory to look for. Scope: the content model — what a folio IS. 1368.title: The no-churn rule
1368.content: Content that has not changed is not rewritten, re-uploaded or re-signed. Each step says how: . | Canonical records. A record is written as JSON with sorted keys, LF line endings and no fetch timestamp inside it. If the canonical bytes equal the held ones, the file is not rewritten. | Content-addressed bitstreams. A bitstream is stored under its SHA-256. An object that already exists is never downloaded, uploaded or overwritten again. | Sorted graph output. The graph is rebuilt in full, and N-Quads partitions are written sorted, so a partition with no changed item comes out byte-identical and is not re-uploaded. | Date-free manifests. bag-info.txt has no Bagging-Date, so the tag manifest of an unchanged payload is byte-identical. | An empty diff ends the run. No commit, no new signature. | . A step that cannot meet its rule reports it. It never hides it.

1369.title: What the agent does
1369.content: . | Plan the initial load as one batch per collection page, with the checkpoint in state/initial-load.json in the Cloudflare git repository. | Review each run report and open a bean for each anomaly: a change count far from the recent median, a quarantined bitstream, a verification whose verdict is unknown, or a partition over its size ceiling. | Never widen scope. Only the owner changes what is exported, its budget or where it is stored. | .

1396.title: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
1396.content: Skill iris-cdn-signing: How an IRIS CDN release is packaged, signed and verified using published standards only: a BagIt bag (RFC 8493), a detached JWS (RFC 7515 App. F) with ES256 (RFC 7518), and the key published in a did:web DID document whose publicKeyJwk carries an x5c chain up to WHO’s signing key. No GDHCN trust list is assumed. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . The code is scripts/iris-cdn/bag.ts and scripts/iris-cdn/signing.ts. The process is processes/iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn.

1397.title: Standards used, and nothing else
1397.content: | Piece | Standard | . | Package and digests | BagIt 1.0, RFC 8493: bagit.txt, bag-info.txt, manifest-sha256.txt, tagmanifest-sha256.txt | . | Signature | JWS compact serialization with a detached payload, RFC 7515 Appendix F | . | Algorithm | ES256, ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256, RFC 7518 §3.4. It is the same curve as WHO’s signing DID key. EdDSA (RFC 8037) is accepted when verifying | . | Public key | JWK, RFC 7517, as publicKeyJwk | . | Trust chain | x5c in the JWK (RFC 7517 §4.7): X.509 certificates, leaf first, ending at one issued by WHO’s signing key | . | Key publication | W3C DID Core 1.0 document, verificationMethod of type JsonWebKey (W3C Controlled Identifiers 1.0) or JsonWebKey2020, which is the form WHO’s own DID uses. Both are accepted | . | DID method | did:web | . No draft standards are used. A new one needs the owner’s explicit approval.

1398.title: What is signed
1398.content: There is one release signature, over the bytes of tagmanifest-sha256.txt, plus one signature per changed library item (below). The tag manifest pins the SHA-256 of every other tag file, and manifest-sha256.txt pins the SHA-256 of every payload file. Signing the tag manifest therefore covers the whole bag. The tag files live in the release git repository; the payload files live in R2 under sha256/<aa>/<digest>. The signature is stored beside the tag manifest as tagmanifest-sha256.txt.jws, in the form <header>..<signature>. The empty middle segment is the detached payload. The protected header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":"did:web:…#<key>"}. ECDSA signatures are randomized. Signing the same bytes twice gives two different signatures, so unchanged content is never re-signed: an unchanged night produces the same tag manifest and gets no new signature.

1399.title: A signature on each library item
1399.content: Every library item has its own manifest at items/<handle>/manifest-sha256.txt, in the same line format as the BagIt payload manifest. It lists the item’s record, records/<handle>.json, and every file under bitstreams/<handle>/. The item’s detached JWS is stored beside it as manifest-sha256.txt.jws. | An item verifies on its own. Fetch its manifest and JWS, verify the JWS against the DID document and its x5c chain, then check each digest. | The release signature proves completeness. The item manifests and their JWSs are payload files, so the release tag manifest pins them all. Nothing can be added or removed without breaking the release signature. | Only changed items are signed. If an item’s manifest bytes did not change, its existing JWS is kept (signItems in scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts). A metadata-only edit changes the record digest, so that item is re-signed while its PDF digest stays the same. | .

1400.title: Where the key comes from
1400.content: The verifier resolves the kid’s DID from the web, never from the package: . | did:web:<cdn-domain> resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/.well-known/did.json, and did:web:<cdn-domain>:iris resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/iris/did.json. The DID must be stable, because the DID is the signer’s identity. | When the DID document lists assertionMethod, the key must be in it. A retired key stays in verificationMethod so that old releases still verify, but it is removed from assertionMethod. A signature by that retired key on a new release then fails. | . If the DID document cannot be fetched, the verdict is unknown, not failed and not verified. A portal that cannot check says so. The trust chain. Our key’s publicKeyJwk.x5c holds the certificates that end at one issued by the key in WHO’s signing DID, did:web:raw.githubusercontent.com:WorldHealthOrganization:tng-participants-prod:main:WHO:signing:DID. The verifier is given WHO’s public key as its anchor, as the variable IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK in CI. With an anchor, a key with no x5c fails. run.ts verify refuses without the anchor or IRIS_CDN_DID: the verdict is unknown and it exits non-zero. Called without anchors, verifyDetached reports the chain as not-checked, never as verified. No other trust anchor is assumed. A trust list, such as GDHCN via WHO SMART Trust, could only be an additional route to the same DID document, never a replacement for it.

1401.title: Key custody and rotation
1401.content: . | The private key is a JWK (kty: EC, crv: P-256, x, y, d). It never goes into git, a log or a bean. It is the GitHub environment secret IRIS_CDN_SIGNING_JWK in environment iris-cdn-release, which only jobs on main can read. | The key already exists. The subordinate key is already published in a DID document, with x5c up to WHO’s signing DID, before the exporter runs. That publication is offline and outside these processes. No CI job issues certificates or edits the DID document. | To rotate: . | Add the new key to the DID document and to assertionMethod. | Publish the DID document. | Sign the next release with the new key. | Take the old key out of assertionMethod, and keep it in verificationMethod. | . | The DID document is built in a fixed order, so republishing it with the same keys writes the same bytes. | .

1402.title: Verifying by hand
1402.content: In a checkout of the release git repository: . # 1. tag files against the tag manifest sha256sum -c tagmanifest-sha256.txt # 2. the release signature, with the key resolved from did:web IRIS_CDN_DID=did:web:<cdn-domain> IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK='<WHO public JWK>' \ bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts verify --release <checkout> --no-revert . Payload digests in manifest-sha256.txt are checked against the objects at https://<cdn-domain>/sha256/<aa>/<digest>, not against files in the checkout.

1404.title: IRIS, DSpace and Dublin Core
1404.content: Skill iris-dspace: How WHO IRIS uses DSpace and qualified Dublin Core — the three identifier systems, MeSH as a controlled vocabulary, bundles, and the containment path — and the requirements a tool reading a record must meet. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Every claim here is read off one captured record: the DSpace full item record for wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng, transcribed at catalogue/records/wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng.dc.json. Nothing is asserted from general knowledge of DSpace. Where this file and the record disagree, the record wins. The type is folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts. It is generic: Dublin Core is ISO 15836 and DSpace is a platform. This file covers only what IRIS does with them.

1405.title: Scale
1405.content: From IRIS’s storage report (By Location → Entire Site) and home page, read 2026-09-20: . |   |   | source | . | items | 273,559 | the home page’s search placeholder | . | files | 1,057,223 | the storage report | . | storage | 361.55 GB | the storage report | . | top-level communities | 8 | the storage report | . Items and files are different denominators, so catalogue/catalogue.json carries them in separate fields, totalItemsUpstream and totalFilesUpstream. That is 3.86 files per item, because an item carries several bitstreams. totalBytesUpstream is derived: the report prints two decimals and no byte count, so the value is round(361.55 × 1024³), good to about ±5 MiB. It is GiB rather than GB because every per-community figure the report prints (238.58, 19.72, 34.84, 26.14, 25.71) reproduces exactly at 2³⁰ and none does at 10⁹.

1406.title: Three identifier systems
1406.content: The worked item carries all three: . | system | value | authoritative? | . | DSpace UUID | 18892cf3-5a4f-42a4-923c-a93f4a594dec | no — IRIS’s own, stable only while this DSpace instance is | . | Handle | 10665/332098 | yes — guaranteed by the Handle System, outside WHO | . | WHO govdoc | WPR/RDO/2020/003 | no — WHO’s publication number | . The library slug wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng is derived from the govdoc, the weakest key. A tool that resolves by Handle survives the source moving. A legacy handle is live in the record, and must not be deduplicated . dc.identifier.uri appears twice: . https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/332098 ← global http://iris.wpro.who.int/handle/10665.1/14518 ← regional, merged away . Regional IRIS instances were folded into the global one and both URIs were kept. The second is a real alternate identifier, and evidence that a source host can disappear (the sourceLoss gate’s worked example).

1407.title: Qualified, repeated, language-tagged
1407.content: Every field is element.qualifier. Four fields repeat in this one record (dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available, dc.identifier.uri, dc.subject.mesh), so Record<string, string> silently keeps the last value and drops the rest. There is a per-field language column, present on dc.title, dc.description and each dc.subject.mesh, absent on the author, the dates and the identifiers. An absent tag is not en: it is a value whose language nobody asserted.

1408.title: MeSH is a controlled vocabulary, not a keyword
1408.content: dc.subject.mesh = Publishing, Guidelines as Topic. These are NLM Medical Subject Headings, with their own identifiers and hierarchy at https://id.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/. A MeSH term can be resolved and subsumed (searching “Guidelines as Topic” should reach narrower terms); a free-text keyword can do neither. DcValue.authority records the distinction per value.

1409.title: An item is not a file: bundles
1409.content: DSpace groups bitstreams into bundles — conventionally ORIGINAL, plus TEXT (extracted), THUMBNAIL and LICENSE. Size and format are per-bitstream: the 2.68 MB in the record is the PDF’s, not the item’s. Bundles are why there are more files than items.

1410.title: Containment is a path, not a parent
1410.content: The breadcrumb: Home → 7. Regional Office for the … → Regional Office for the W… → Information products — four levels, two of them communities and one a collection. DSpace also lets an item be mapped into several collections, so “the” parent of a node does not exist. CatalogueNode.parents is a list of paths.

1411.title: What a later tool needs — as requirements
1411.content: | # | requirement | why, in one line | . | R1 | Resolve by Handle where one exists; treat UUID and govdoc as secondary | only the Handle is guaranteed outside WHO | . | R2 | Never deduplicate dc.identifier.uri | the second one is evidence of a host that vanished | . | R3 | Preserve repetition on every field, not a known list | four fields repeat in a single record; assume more do | . | R4 | Treat an absent language as unasserted, never as en | both states occur in one record | . | R5 | Carry dc.subject.mesh as a controlled value with its authority | it can be resolved and subsumed; a keyword cannot | . | R6 | Model bitstreams per bundle, with size and format on the bitstream | an item is not a file | . | R7 | Model containment as a list of paths | four levels deep, and multiple mappings are legal | . | R8 | Never infer metadata from the PDF when a record exists | OCR off a title page catalogued the WHO Editorial Style Manual as Abies | . | R9 | Record what the source says even when it contradicts the file | dc.description says 30 p.; the PDF has 33 | . | R10 | An item with no known collection carries parents: [] — never a guessed one | held-and-unplaceable is a STATE; inventing containment is unfalsifiable | . | R11 | Key a node by path when its UUID is not in the capture | an invented UUID resolves to nothing while looking authoritative | . | R12 | Keep the page captured and the identifier apart | /items/<uuid>/full is what was fetched; the Handle is what the item IS | . | R13 | A materialized claim must name bytes that EXIST, and something must check it | an unchecked claim can name no bytes and still pass as held | . | R14 | Read a storage figure in the units that round-trip its own bytes | IRIS prints “GB” for what its byte counts make GiB — a 7% error | . | R15 | Never fall back to a parent URL when an item has no upstream URI | “no upstream URI recorded” is the answer; the front page is a lie that resolves | . | R16 | A partial transcription must SAY it is partial | a truncated abstract that does not declare itself cannot be told from a short one | . | R17 | Hold what you hold: model the bitstreams whose bytes are here | the handbook lists 8 upstream; this repository has 1 | . | R18 | Do not “correct” a record that looks wrong | the English-titled editorial manual really does carry an Italian ISBN | . | R19 | A derived figure must round-trip the figure it was derived from | round(361.55 × 1024³) bytes must render back as 361.55 GiB | . | R20 | An item count and a file count are different denominators | 273,559 against 1,057,223 — a fraction built from the wrong one is off by 3.86× | . | R21 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (Upstream Skolemization) | minting https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} at extraction leaves no blank nodes for a later pass to resolve | . | R22 | Append-only streaming partition writes | A 300,000 item corpus cannot accumulate uncompressed in working memory; write quads directly to partition file streams | . R8: where a library entry’s title comes from . who-pub-tps-931 shows why. Its structure.json carries title: "Abies" and authors_raw: "Cpe N" — OCR noise off a scanned title page of the WHO Editorial Style Manual. 9789241548960-eng has three renderings of one title from the PDF (Handbook forGuideline Development 2nd edition from joined title lines, GRC Handbook - second edition from PDF docinfo, and the real one) and no authority among them. The IRIS record settles both. A library entry’s title is taken, in order, from: . | the catalogue record: dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming the entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef; | referenced.json identity.title; | the PDF Info /Title (structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title), only when it is not junk such as Microsoft Word - …, a file name, untitled, or an arXiv stamp; | the slug, which check:library-qa then reports as title-missing. | . The page-1 front-matter parse is never a title. It may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. The manifest records which source won as meta.title_source (for example dc-record) and where it came from as meta.title_from, so R8 can be checked. The resolver is cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts; the library-ingestion skill carries the full rule.

1412.title: Covers: an artefact we made, filed where IRIS files its own
1412.content: The replica’s home page shows a cover beside each item in its Recent Submissions strip, and each library entry page shows it too. None of them came from IRIS. Each is page 1 of the item’s PDF, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py and filed as a THUMBNAIL-bundle bitstream — the bundle name DSpace uses for the thumbnails it generates. Nothing downstream can tell the two apart from the bundle name, so the bitstream’s materialization.note must say the cover was derived here. The PDF is either held in this repository or, for a referenced item, fetched by the iris-cover-pdfs GitHub workflow, matched against the sha256 its ORIGINAL bitstream records, rendered and discarded. Only the cover PNG is committed. folio-assistant-core/scripts/gen-covers.ts (bun run iris:covers) renders only covers the catalogue asks for: a node declares the THUMBNAIL bitstream and the script supplies the bytes. It refuses to write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation, since a tool cannot attest to its own output. bun run iris:covers:check compares the bytes, the recorded sha256 and the recorded pixel dimensions, re-rendering where the PDF is held. That is R13 for covers. A cover whose PDF is not held can be verified but not re-rendered. The WHO emblem is masked on covers . The site chrome carries no WHO mark until the replica is published under WHO. Covers are shown with the WHO emblem and wordmark blanked to flat grey before the PNG is written, so the committed bytes never contain it. Each THUMBNAIL bitstream declares the blanked rectangles and the reason as maskedRegions. A title that contains “WHO” is not masked: it is the work’s name. A cover whose publication gates block it is shown as cover withheld, not no cover.

1413.title: Getting a record
1413.content: DSpace 7 exposes /server/api/discover/search/objects, paged and filterable by dsoType, scope and facets; communities are listed at /community-list. The calls this repository makes, and what live IRIS accepts, are in iris-rest-feed; the code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts. A record derived from a PDF rather than transcribed from IRIS must be marked derived, so it can be replaced wholesale when the real record arrives with nothing downstream having believed it. Enumeration cost, subsetting and the characterisation that decides whether IRIS may be cited at all are in who-iris/sources/who-iris.json.

1415.title: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
1415.content: Skill iris-oxigraph: How to build WHO IRIS catalogue and Qualified Dublin Core metadata into partitioned N-Quads, and query it with Oxigraph — in Bun on the build side, in WebAssembly in the browser — including cross-graph joins and facet counts. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . The IRIS catalogue and its Dublin Core records are compiled into named graphs and queried with Oxigraph: natively in Bun at build time, and as WebAssembly in a browser. One SPARQL query can then join Dublin Core properties, catalogue containment and bitstream access gates — which DSpace Discovery cannot do in a single call.

1416.title: Build and query
1416.content: # Build from catalogue/nodes and site/dublin-core into dist/oxigraph/ bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts # Build from exported DSpace records (the CDN release's records/ tree) bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts --records <dir> --out <dir> # Load dist/oxigraph/who-iris-dataset.nq and run sample searches and facets bun run scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts exports IrisOxigraphEngine (loadSpine, loadCommunity, searchSpine, complexSearch, facetCounts). The CDN exporter (scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts) calls the build over exported records and publishes each output file as graph/<file>.

1417.title: 1. Graphs and files
1417.content: The build writes, sorted and de-duplicated so unchanged inputs give byte-identical files: . | Tier 1, the spine — <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine>, in who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz. Hierarchy (dspace:Community, dspace:Collection), item Handles, titles, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. Loaded first. | Tier 2, one partition per community — <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}>, in iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz. The full Dublin Core of that community’s items: MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial coverage, govdoc numbers, ISBNs. Mounted on demand. | Catalogue and metadata graphs — <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> and <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata>, each in its own iris_who_int_graph_{catalogue,metadata}.nq(.gz), and merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz for server-side use and integrity checks. | subgraph-manifest.json — the spine and each community partition, with file names, quad counts and item counts. | queries.json — prepared SPARQL queries. | . Namespaces . | dspace: = https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace# — catalogue terms (Item, inCommunity, hasBitstream, fileName, …). | dspaceNs: = https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/ — Dublin Core value terms, including authority. | . No binary bytes in the graph . PDFs, cover images and archives are never stored as literals. A bitstream node carries only: . | dspace:fileName (e.g. "WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf") | dspace:mediaType (e.g. "application/pdf") | dspace:fileBytes (integer) | dspace:copyrightGate — the copyright gate’s verdict, e.g. "permitted" | . The bytes are fetched from the CDN.

1418.title: 2. Requirements
1418.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | OX-1 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx}); the build fails if any blank node remains | no multi-document collisions, every node addressable, no normalizer pass | . | OX-2 | Store zero binary bytes in RDF | keeps WASM memory small; binaries are static files on the CDN | . | OX-3 | Join across named graphs with explicit GRAPH blocks | separates containment and rights from bibliographic description | . | OX-4 | Use Handle URIs as the item subject (https://hdl.handle.net/...) | identity resolves outside WHO’s servers | . | OX-5 | Treat bitstream rights as access gates | results can be filtered by whether the PDF may be downloaded | . | OX-6 | Partition by community | a client fetches only the slice it needs | . | OX-7 | Never scan whole-corpus text in SPARQL | full text belongs in a static inverted index | . | OX-8 | Preserve controlled-vocabulary authorities (dspaceNs:authority) | distinguishes MeSH headings from free keywords | . | OX-9 | Append-only streaming partition emission | bounded memory at 300,000 items. Not met yet: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is defined but unused | .

1419.title: 3. SPARQL recipes
1419.content: Recipe 1: multi-condition search . Items in the Western Pacific community, issued in or after 2000, with a subject containing “guidelines”, and a PDF whose copyright verdict is permitted. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX dspace: <https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> SELECT DISTINCT ?handle ?title ?creator ?issued ?pdfName WHERE { # 1. Join Dublin Core Metadata GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:creator ?crNode ; dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?crNode rdf:value ?creator . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?handle dcterms:issued ?issued } } # 2. Join Catalogue Hierarchy & Access Gates GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> { ?handle dspace:inCommunity ?comm ; dspace:hasBitstream ?bs . ?comm rdfs:label ?commLabel . ?bs dspace:mediaType "application/pdf" ; dspace:fileName ?pdfName ; dspace:copyrightGate "permitted" . } # 3. Multi-Field Filter Evaluation BIND(IF(BOUND(?issued), xsd:integer(SUBSTR(STR(?issued), 1, 4)), 0) AS ?year) FILTER ( CONTAINS(LCASE(?subject), "guidelines") && CONTAINS(LCASE(?commLabel), "western pacific") && (?year >= 2000) ) } ORDER BY DESC(?year) . Recipe 2: facet counts . Item counts per subject term and its authority. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX dspaceNs: <https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/> SELECT ?subject (COUNT(DISTINCT ?handle) AS ?itemCount) ?authority WHERE { GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?sNode dspaceNs:authority ?authority } } } GROUP BY ?subject ?authority ORDER BY DESC(?itemCount) ?subject .

1420.title: 4. Browser pattern: spine first, communities on demand
1420.content: import oxigraph from 'oxigraph'; // Where the graph files are served from, e.g. a release's graph/ directory. const BASE = '<graph-base-url>'; async function gunzipText(resp: Response): Promise<string> { const stream = resp.body!.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream('gzip')); return new Response(stream).text(); } const store = new oxigraph.Store(); // 1. Fetch the spine and the manifest const [spineResp, manifestResp] = await Promise.all([ fetch(`${BASE}/who-iris-spine.nq.gz`), fetch(`${BASE}/subgraph-manifest.json`), ]); const manifest = await manifestResp.json(); // 2. Load the spine: hierarchy, title search and rights filtering work now store.load(await gunzipText(spineResp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); // 3. Mount a community when the user selects it. load() adds its named // graph without clobbering what is already in the store. async function mountCommunity(commId: string) { const partition = manifest.tiers.tier2_communities.partitions[commId]; if (!partition) return; const resp = await fetch(`${BASE}/${partition.fileGz}`); store.load(await gunzipText(resp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); } // 4. Run a prepared query locally for (const binding of store.query(myPreparedQuery)) { console.log(binding.get('title').value); } .

1422.title: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
1422.content: Skill iris-rest-feed: How to read changes from the WHO IRIS DSpace 7 REST API: the nightly “changed since” walk over Discovery, the weekly reconciliation that stands in for the deletions REST does not report, and the guard that stops a short listing from reading as a mass withdrawal. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Changes are read from the DSpace REST API only. REST has no change feed with deletions, so a nightly walk is paired with a weekly reconciliation. The code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts; its tests run on fixtures in scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts.

1423.title: What live IRIS accepts
1423.content: . | Discovery offers only five sortOptions: score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available. sort=lastModified,DESC returns HTTP 422. | Changes are found with a Solr range query instead: query=lastModified:[<isoZ> TO *]. | The bound must be a Z-suffixed UTC timestamp. A +00:00 offset returns totalElements: 0. | .

1424.title: Endpoints
1424.content: | Use | Request | . | Changed items since cursor | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&query=lastModified:[{isoZ} TO *]&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Weekly full item listing | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Collection-scoped batch (initial load) | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&scope={collectionUuid}&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Communities / collections with parent | GET /server/api/core/{communities|collections}?page=N&size=100&embed=parentCommunity | . | One item with its files and collection | GET /server/api/core/items/{uuid}?embed=bundles/bitstreams&embed=owningCollection | . | Bundle bitstreams beyond page 0 | GET /server/api/core/bundles/{bundleUuid}/bitstreams?page=N&size=100 | . | A file’s bytes | GET /server/api/core/bitstreams/{uuid}/content | .

1425.title: Nightly: changedSince(cursor)
1425.content: . | Normalise cursor to UTC Z (new Date(Date.parse(cursor)).toISOString()) and run the range query above. | Page through the matching result set. | The cursor is inclusive: an item modified at that instant is read again, not missed. Re-reading an unchanged item writes the same bytes. | Return the items oldest first, de-duplicated by UUID. | . The cursor is the newest lastModified read, kept in state/cursor.json. A failed night does not advance it.

1426.title: Metadata changes without the PDF changing
1426.content: A PDF may stay the same while its Dublin Core changes. Records and files are handled separately: . | A record is re-read whenever its item appears in the walk. A PDF is re-fetched only if its DSpace MD5 changed. | Communities and collections are re-read in full every night (allContainers). A renamed collection changes no item, and DSpace 7 does not expose lastModified for these. An unchanged one serializes to the same bytes. | The weekly metadata check. The weekly listing pages carry each item’s metadata. metadataSha hashes it canonically, and any item whose hash differs from the one last ingested is re-read. That catches edits that did not move lastModified, without one fetch per item. | .

1427.title: Weekly: allItems and withdrawnOrHidden
1427.content: . | List every item ID Discovery returns. | Compare that list with the IDs the library holds. | Guard. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Possible causes are a paging fault, an outage or a Solr reindex. | Re-fetch each missing item by ID. Mark it withdrawn only if IRIS confirms it: withdrawn: true, or a 404 (gone), 401 or 403 (private). | .

1428.title: Fixity
1428.content: DSpace reports an MD5 checkSum for each bitstream. Downloaded bytes must match it before their SHA-256 is recorded. A mismatch quarantines the bitstream and reports it. It is never retried silently.

1429.title: Politeness
1429.content: Requests are made one at a time, with a User-Agent that names the project and its repository, and back off on 429 and 503. The initial load is paced to the budget stated in Task_StateBudget (processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn), including maxRequestsPerSecond.

1430.title: A subset by reference: run.ts subset
1430.content: bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset catalogues part of IRIS without fetching any bytes (who-iris#207): for each item, the Dublin Core record as DSpace returns it and a referenced catalogue node whose ORIGINAL bitstreams link to https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/{uuid}/download. The subsets it reads live in scripts/iris-cdn/subsets/. | Which items. A handles file goes first (for example the IRIS items a DAK cites), then a Discovery query. The query is a field query on metadata (dc.title, dc.subject, dc.subject.mesh, dc.description.abstract), not a bare keyword. A bare keyword also searches the PDF text, so vaccine matches a report that mentions one in passing. | Write boolean operators in capitals. Solr reads a lowercase or as a word: HIV or immunization or vaccine matches fewer items than vaccine alone. | A Handle to an item: GET /server/api/pid/find?id=hdl:{handle} answers 302 to /server/api/core/items/{uuid}. | An ISBN or govdoc to an item: query=dc.identifier.isbn:"{isbn13}" or query=dc.identifier.govdoc:"WHO/HIV/2017.09". | A sample is one-row pages at seeded random offsets, so the same seed gives the same items. | No fixity is claimed. IRIS reports an MD5. A sha256 is recorded only once the bytes are fetched (R13), so the MD5 goes in the bitstream’s note. | Hand-made nodes win. An item whose Handle or UUID another node already carries is skipped and reported. The tool rewrites only its own nodes, the ones whose note starts “Catalogued by reference by scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset”, and only when they changed. | A token, when IRIS gives one, comes from the IRIS_DSPACE_TOKEN environment variable as Authorization: Bearer …. It never appears in an argument, a file or a log. | .
