1476.title: Prepare-merge — get a feature branch ready to land
1476.content: Skill prepare-merge: Take a feature branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises: base merged in, generated files regenerated, the folio’s content-type gates run, then pushed. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Canonical, repo-agnostic recipe for taking a claude/* (or any feature) branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises. Downstream repositories vendor or sync it rather than maintaining their own copy. “Prepare-merge” is a plain-English ask, not a built-in command, so without one recipe each agent re-derives the steps, inconsistently or unsafely. “Prepare-merge” ≠ “merge”. It makes the branch mergeable and stops. It does not push to the default branch and does not merge a PR. Both are outward-facing, hard-to-reverse actions — do them only on an explicit request. The merge itself is its own sub-process with its own gate, merge-to-main: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for THAT merge, recorded, then the merge. Asking for prepare-merge (or “ship it”) is not that authorisation.

1477.title: fsh-guts must not reach publication
1477.content: Before a branch that touches the knowledge graph ships, the published export must contain no reference to fsh-guts — not the graph typology, not the declared directory, not the skill that documents it, and not an edge naming any of them. scripts/tests/fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts asserts it against the built artefact and runs in bun test. The mechanism is in kg-export §”fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph”.

1478.title: Recipe
1478.content: . | Clean + committed. git status --short must be empty. Commit outstanding work first (the container is ephemeral — uncommitted work is lost on resume). | Fetch the base + your branch (retry on network error, backoff 2/4/8/16s): git fetch origin <base> <branch>. | Integrate if the base moved. Compare git merge-base HEAD origin/<base> to git rev-parse origin/<base>: . | Equal → base hasn’t moved; nothing to do (your branch is a clean fast-forward). | Different → bring the base in, resolve conflicts, then re-run the green check. A rebase needs a force-push with lease: git push --force-with-lease — never a bare --force (it clobbers sibling pushes). | . Merge with bun run cat merge:main, never a plain git merge followed by regen. It resolves every conflict a declared pattern covers (glossaries, translated glossaries, UML, viewer pages, site data, QA sidecars), refuses the rest with the tree restored, and runs regen on the result. A plain git merge stops on those same generated files, one by one. After EVERY base merge, conflicted or not, run bun run cat regen — see §”A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact” below. If you merged with bun run cat merge:main, its regen already was that run; do not run a second one. For a merge whose conflicts were all generated, the round is merge-conflict-patterns §”A merge round — run each check ONCE”: targeted checks and a push, with CI’s sharded run as the full gate set in place of a local bun run cat gates or check:merged. An authored conflict, or a merge that touched code, still owes both. A conflict in test/results/ or test/attestations/: see §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/” below before resolving either by hand. | Prove it merges cleanly (no assumptions): . | git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<base> HEAD → success means a clean fast-forward, so conflicts are impossible. This alone is sufficient. | Otherwise dry-run with git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base> HEAD (exit 0 = clean; non-zero = not clean; add --name-only to list the conflicted paths) and trust its exit code AND its first line. Exit 1 means CONFLICT only when stdout opens with the merged tree’s id — git also exits 1 for a ref it cannot merge (unfetched, mistyped), printing no tree, and that is “could not determine”, never “conflicted with nothing in conflict”. | Capture $? on the line after the command, before anything else runs — git merge-tree … >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?, or cmd || rc=$?. echo "base($(git rev-parse --short origin/main)) rc=$?" reports the SUBSTITUTION’s status, always 0 when the ref exists. if ! cmd; then rc=$? is the same trap: inside that branch $? is ! cmd’s status, 0. shell-exit-status.test.ts fails on either shape in a tracked script or workflow. | GitHub’s HTTP 405 “Pull Request has merge conflicts” is a backstop, not a check — it is learned at merge time, after the PR was announced clean. Do not grep the old three-arg output for <<<<<<< / “changed in both”: that false-positives on files which legitimately contain those literals (docs about merge conflicts, test fixtures, this skill). | A clean text merge is not a clean state. merge-tree answers “do the files conflict?”, not “do the gates pass on the result?”. Before asking for a merge, run bun run cat check:merged: it builds the merge with the current base in a throwaway worktree and runs the full bun run cat gates there (exit 0 passes, 1 fails, 2 could not determine — never read as clean). A generated measurement can be green on the branch, green on the base, merge without a conflict, and be stale on the result. | GitHub’s merge queue tests exactly the commit that will land; the gating workflows carry merge_group: so it works once the owner turns it on. Until then, check:merged is the agent’s half. | . | Green check. Run the project’s tests/build (here: bun test, plus bun build <file> --target=bun for type-checking touched files). Report honestly: distinguish failures you caused from pre-existing ones (diff the counts against a baseline run on the merge-base). Do not call a branch green by silently inheriting red. Then run bun run cat security:gate, by name, and quote its result. It runs every security check this repository has (workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile and toolchain pins, QA reviewer permission, materialised fixity) plus two advisories, and refuses when a blocking check fails OR could not be run. Most of those checks are also inside bun run cat gates; naming the command here makes the merge step cover security explicitly, rather than only when the CI run before it happened to include it. Its advisories (unpinned third-party actions, dependency advisories) are reported in the PR and are not cleared by a green gate. Check the adversarial review verdict with bun run cat check:adversarial-review. On any branch with agent provenance (trailers, claude/* branch, bot committer), it verifies that an independent adversarial review verdict exists, binds to the head SHA, and covers the full diff without silent truncation. Findings are warn-only (“would have blocked”): they are recorded, as data for deciding when to promote the check to a gate, and do not hold the merge. Know what the target covered. Green is a claim about the files the build compiled, which is usually fewer than the files on disk — build targets default to a root plus its transitive imports. Confirm the files you touched were in it (artifact count vs. source count, or build the module by name), and scope any corpus-wide number you quote to what actually ran. For contentType: paper branches that touch content blocks, also run the block_pdf_render gate: . bun run scripts/render-changed-blocks.ts [--upload-drive] . This compiles a standalone PDF for every changed block and scrapes the LaTeX log; --upload-drive additionally pushes clean PDFs to Google Drive when it is configured. Exits 1 on LaTeX errors (fix required); exits 0 with warnings only (advisory); exits 2 on setup problems — including no local latexmk, which is the common case in a container. Exit 2 means the gate did not run; report it that way rather than folding it into a green. For a branch that changes a folio’s blocks, report review coverage. content-change-review.bpmn’s coverage gate (GW_Covered, table decisions/review-coverage-gate.dmn) reads the block counts below and, where the preview published a rendered-impact.json, three page counts (unreviewed pages, undetermined inputs, missed pages; see rendered-impact). Report them in the PR body, in the gate’s own terms, and a page count the preview did not publish as “not known”: . | open defects: review comments of kind defect still open or addressed, from the preview’s review-comments.json; | changed blocks with neither a verdict nor a waiver on their current version. | . Both come from one command, the folio-review-coverage Tool, run on the preview’s published files with --changeset changeset.json --blocks blocks.json --comments review-comments.json [--rendered rendered-impact.json --measured rendered-measured.json]. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that owns the review process. Quote its stderr summary. If the preview has no review-comments.json, or one with no verdicts field, write “not measured”, never 0. Never count resolved comments as coverage: a resolved comment is not a reviewer’s verdict on the block. This REPORTS; it does not merge or refuse. The gate belongs to the review process, and the committee decides the outcome. Say so when coverage could not be measured, because a branch passed with unmeasured coverage reads as “reviewed”. | Push the feature branch (retry/backoff as in step 2): git push -u origin <branch>. Then ask whether the push produced a run: bun run cat check:head-has-run. The push runs the fast gates first, where the pre-push hook is on. Git’s pre-push hook (installed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/install.sh) and, for agents, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on git push both run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pre-push-gates.ts on the checked-out tree, before anything leaves the container (work items cat-tools-pp9g and folio-assistant-fn8q). It runs the fast gates minus the whole-suite bun test, plus only the test files whose import closure holds a file the push changed (owner, 2026-11-05: “Affected tests only”). CI still runs the whole suite. What it says: . | refused: a gate or an affected test that is green on the push’s base in this same environment is red now. Fix it, as you would a red CI job. It quotes the gates or tests and the log path; | ? gates not judged: a red it cannot attribute to this push (red on the base too, or no base outcomes recorded here), tracked files that differ from HEAD, exit 2, or no cat runner. The push goes and CI decides. A fresh container reddens some tests CI passes (no publish-time pages, a slower machine), so this is not a local green: report it as not determined, never as pass; | ✓: the fast gates passed on this tree and the affected tests with them. A record keyed by the tree is written; it names bun test as held out, so it never claims the suite. Pushing the same tree again re-runs nothing. | . A push the hook refused is never forced through with a bare --no-verify. If you must push anyway, name the reason, which is logged to .git/cat-gates/push.log: CAT_GATES_BYPASS='<reason>' git push ..., and put the same reason in the PR body. A local pass does not replace step 7: CI still runs every gate. This does not change what you do next — step 7 dispatches either way. It changes what you can honestly SAY. A push can silently produce no run, and a pull request showing zero checks is indistinguishable from one whose checks have not started (§Guardrails, “NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”). If the check reports no run, write that in the PR body alongside the dispatched run’s URL. Three states, and the third is not a finding: could not ask (no remote, no network, 403, 404) means nothing was established, and it must not be reported as either answer. | Dispatch the repo’s CI on the pushed branch, and fold the result into the PR. Local green is not CI green — CI runs on a cold cache, its own toolchain, and without whatever build flags you set locally. So after the push, trigger the relevant workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <wf>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and put the run URL and conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. Do not open a PR citing a workflow nobody ran. If you lack actions: write and dispatch returns 403, do not quietly skip it: state in the PR that CI was not run, and give the exact command a maintainer should run. Find the workflow by reading .github/workflows/, not by name. Guessing a workflow name is how this gate gets skipped while appearing to run (a guessed name can be a publish workflow). In a repository whose workflows are all workflow_dispatch-only, nothing runs on push or PR, and “CI is green” is only ever true because someone dispatched it. Check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): “there is a workflow” is not evidence anything is being checked. Many workflows document a local equivalent in their own header. Run those; they are the same check without the dispatch. Read the workflow before assuming there is no local path. | Stop here unless a PR / merge was explicitly requested. If a PR was requested, see below. | .

1479.title: What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim
1479.content: The same commit can fail different tests in CI, in a clean worktree, and when the failing files are run alone, and the sets need not be nested. A green local run is not a weaker version of a green CI run — it is a different measurement, and either can be the one that is wrong. What it entitles you to say, exactly: . The gates I ran passed, on the tree I ran them on, in this environment. And what it does not entitle: . | “CI will pass.” CI tests refs/pull/N/merge, not your head — a tree neither parent holds. A staleness that exists only in the merge tree cannot be seen from any checkout. | “The gate set passed.” Only if you ran the gate set. A subset chosen by hand misses gates such as check:partition (a new script must be classified in scripts/partition/instance-rules.ts) and no check script is unrun (a new check:* needs a SCRIPT_EXEMPTIONS entry when no workflow runs it — or, for a script owned by a layer above cat-harness, a gateExemptions.scripts row in that layer’s <instance>.json). bun run cat gates derives its list from the workflow, so it cannot drift from what CI runs. | “Nothing is failing, so nothing is wrong.” A conflicted head produces no merge ref, so pull_request workflows never fire and the PR shows zero check runs. That reads as untested, not as red. | “It passed in isolation, so the failure is not mine.” Running the file alone removes the only condition under which it failed — for example a test near its time budget that crosses it only under load. | . Your environment is part of the claim, and it can be checked. Run bun run cat check:environment before trusting a run from any hand-built tree, and install dependencies rather than borrowing them: a symlinked root node_modules makes any tool that resolves a real path through it report a location this repository does not contain. Confirming the symlink is git-ignored is not enough; path resolution is a separate confound.

1480.title: A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream (STRICT)
1480.content: A layer that adds a gate or a check:* script takes on its downstream layers too (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Rule 13”: add it): the next re-pin of each one runs it. Twice on 2026-11-07 a lower layer’s main broke every downstream re-pin. New check scripts that no downstream workflow ran failed no check script is unrun (check:test-gherkin, and translation:page-qa:check, which also had a flag mismatch). Checks that walked the file tree without skipping declared build outputs failed too (two such checks in the tools layer). Each time, the re-pin became the P0. So, in the same PR that adds the gate: . | It passes on the layer’s own main. | It says how downstream layers run it: either wired through the shared reusable workflow, or declared opt-in per layer with an exemption row each downstream layer can carry. | A downstream dry run proves it: lay the branch over a fresh mount of folio-assistant main, and run the gate set there. Say in the PR what ran and its result. | . Without all three, the gate waits. It never lands for the next re-pin to discover.

1481.title: A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact (STRICT)
1481.content: bun run cat regen after every base merge. Not only after a conflicted one — after every one. bun run cat merge:main runs it as part of the merge, so after merge:main it has already happened once and a second run re-asks the same tree. Two branches can change one committed generated file in non-overlapping places — say one adds a count field to a projection’s header and the other adds an entry to its array. Git merges them with no conflict and produces an artefact neither side would ever emit (a count that disagrees with the list). A conflict is a question. A clean merge is an assertion that the result is correct — and for a generated file that assertion is worth nothing, because git is merging text it has no way to evaluate. After a merge, RE-RUN THE GENERATORS. Never read the diff to decide whether you need to. bun run cat regen does it by asking each gate first, so its output is the set of artefacts the merge actually broke rather than a wholesale rewrite: . bun run cat regen # repair what is stale in the whole gate set bun run cat regen --fast # ...only the jobs that install no browser bun run cat regen --dry-run # report what is stale, change nothing bun run cat regen --changed <base> # ask only the pairs whose inputs changed since <base> bun run cat regen --explain # say, per pair, why it was asked or not . It asks the gates rather than regenerating everything because the gates (read from the workflow, not package.json) are the list, and because rewriting artefacts that were already correct leaves a diff that says nothing about what the merge broke. The QA working copy is part of the run — do not build it by hand around regen. Generators such as uml:overview and readme:subgraphs read the computed, ignored */test/results/ tree. Before every pass regen asks the copy’s stamp (bun run cat qa:working-copy -- --status) whether it was built from the tree as it stands, and rebuilds it if not. The paths that rebuild changed join the pass’s change set, so any pair that reads them is asked again. A failed build exits 2, and regen never grades a pass over a half-built copy. gates uses the same stamp, so the gates that follows a regen on the same tree builds nothing. It reports four states, and unrepaired is the one to read: a check that still fails after its writer ran is a real defect, not staleness, and the command exits non-zero rather than claiming a repair it did not make. So is a check with no writer. --changed asks less, and says what it assumed. A pair whose declared inputs, script sources and commands meet none of the paths changed since <base> (plus the working tree) is not asked: its answer is its answer at <base>. Undeclared and {tracked} pairs are always asked, as is any pair whose inputs cannot be determined. bun run cat merge:main passes the merge’s fork point, so a skipped pair is one NEITHER side touched, and it is current if the fork point, the branch tip or the base tip was current. merge:main -- --full-regen asks every pair. Separately, every pass after the first asks only the pairs whose inputs the previous pass actually changed (measured from git, not declared). Both cuts are only as good as the task-io.ts declarations — and, for a task owned by a layer above cat-harness, that layer’s own taskIo block in its <instance>.json. task-io.ts collects them and refuses a task declared twice, so declare a row where its script lives, never in both places. The whole-tree pairs (kg:audit:all:check, skill:register:check, kg:audit:check) still run after every merge. Submodules: check the pointers BEFORE you stage the merge (STRICT) . A base merge can roll a submodule back without a conflict, and git add -A is how. git merge updates a submodule’s gitlink in the index but not the submodule’s working checkout. If the checkout still sits at the branch’s old pointer, git add -A during conflict resolution stages that stale checkout, rolling the submodule back in the merge commit. bun run cat regen then runs against the old tools and “repairs” generated files to their old form, and CI fails in code the PR never touched. No step conflicts, and every local check against the stale submodule passes. So, after any base merge and before staging: . git submodule update --init --recursive # move each checkout to the merged pointer git diff --cached --submodule=short -- bootstrap bootstrap-tools # must be empty unless YOU bumped it . Then regenerate. Stage paths by name during a merge, never git add -A, and before pushing confirm the merge carries only your change: . git diff --stat origin/<base> HEAD # should list your files, not hundreds . A diff against the base far larger than your PR is the signal.

1482.title: Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/ — regenerate one, read the other
1482.content: | tree | holds | durable home | on a conflict | . | <instance>/test/results/** | DERIVED verdicts — every script entry | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ and pr/<n>/<sha>/, written by the CI job qa-publish | take the base’s side: bun run cat merge:main does, then bun run cat regen | . | <instance>/test/attestations/** | JUDGEMENTS — every agent, human and baseline-pair attestation, qa-attestations/v1 | main, as authored content | a person reads both sides; never regenerated, never “take ours” | . test/results/ files are not committed on main, so a base merge conflicts there only for a branch that still carries a copy. merge:main takes the base’s side (the derived-results pattern in merge-conflict-patterns), which is the deletion, and regen rewrites the working copy. Do not hand-resolve one and do not regenerate one in order to “commit the result”: the record of a commit is its qa-reports entry, which no merge touches. Regenerating is a resolution, not a guess, because both writers are idempotent (sameScriptVerdict keeps a reproduced entry verbatim and ignores reviewed_at, reviewed_sha and script_commit_sha), so a sidecar is a pure function of the tree. A conflict in test/attestations/ is two judgements that disagree, and reconciling them is a person’s call. No merge-conflict pattern names that tree, so merge:main refuses it, as does qa:attestations:migrate. Keep both sides’ entries unless they are the same judgement; then run bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate:check, which exits 1 if a judgement is still only in a derived file. There is no qa:resolve-conflicts command: derived sidecars are not committed, so there is nothing for it to resolve.

1483.title: A change that moves a cached step’s key — publish what CI can verify
1483.content: If the change moves the key of an exact cached step whose producer the determinism audit lists as DETERMINISTIC, run bun run cat cache:publish <step> before pushing, so CI only verifies the entry instead of rebuilding it. Today that is cat-mount when index.lock.json changes. Verdicts are never published this way. The rule, the trust classes and the budget are in cache-first-ci.

1484.title: Shipping is not merging — hand over on the PR itself
1484.content: What happens after the handover is merge-to-main, called by merge-train.bpmn for a queued PR and by crdm-close.bpmn for a CRDM feature. When the branch is green and pushed, it reaches the Merge Steward only by its own state: label ready-to-merge, a signed ready: <head sha> comment, and no needs-merge-human. merge-queue §”Handing a PR to the queue” has the six points, and when NOT to spend CI keeping up while far back. The PR’s state is the record. The request to merge is a message: send the merge manager the six-line merge request of merge-manager-watcher §”The merge request: six lines”, with the PR URL, the session URL, what changed, the rendered preview and what to look for in it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Never merge it yourself, and never re-pin to make it green: send repin+merge: instead (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). A lone session is elected merge manager alone, so it posts the same six lines in its own chat, then asks the owner by card.

1485.title: Opening the PR (only when asked)
1485.content: GitHub access here is via the GitHub MCP server, whose tools are deferred (lazy-loaded). At session start they appear as names only — you cannot call them until you load the schema: . ToolSearch "select:mcp__github__create_pull_request" . Then call mcp__github__create_pull_request with owner, repo, head (the feature branch), base. This “load-then-call” round-trip is by design, not a failure, and is needed once per deferred tool per session, for every mcp__github__* tool (review, comment, merge, CI status). PR body content: pr-description, written for a first-time reader. PR body convention: end with the Claude Code footer + session link (see the harness git instructions). Do not include the model identifier in the PR.

1486.title: Guardrails
1486.content: . | Never push to the default branch and never merge a PR without an explicit ask. Prepare-merge leaves the decision to the human. When the ask comes, the merge runs merge-to-main; a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green” is not the ask. | In folio-assistant an agent never merges to main at all. When CI is green on every job: mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha>. The Merge Steward session brings main in, regenerates and merges. If it reports red: fix, then re-label. The policy is in continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”. | Check the change against the skills that govern it before calling it ready, an agent’s PR above all. Green CI says the code does what its tests say; it does not say the change keeps the rules the owner set for that area. Read the governing skills (from the mounted layers when the MCP skill server is unreachable) and hold the diff to them: a step that, say, copies the IG Publisher’s finished HTML into a site passes every test and breaks ig-render-jekyll. A design choice the PR body describes in passing is a question for the owner when a skill already answers it, never an implementation detail to merge past. | --force-with-lease, never bare --force when a rebase rewrote history. | Honest green. Pre-existing red is reported as pre-existing, with evidence; your-change red blocks the “ready” claim. | NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN — verify against the run list, never the PR page. A PR with zero check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Both are “nothing red”. A push followed by a PR can produce no pull_request-event run for that head, the newest run on the branch being for the previous head. Waiting longer is not the remedy, because how long you wait does not predict whether a run appears, and neither is avoiding force-pushes: plain fast-forwards hit it too. So before calling a branch ready, and before any merge: . | Read mergeable_state FIRST — and believe it only when it says dirty. clean can be served stale (a merged PR’s pre-merge view), and unknown means GitHub has not finished computing it. dirty is the one value worth acting on unilaterally, because its remedy — merging the base in — costs nothing on a PR that did not need it. dirty means the PR conflicts with its base, which is very likely why nothing ran: a workflow on: pull_request: with actions/checkout@v4 and no ref: checks out refs/pull/N/merge, and a conflicting PR has no such commit. When it is dirty, merge the base branch in — do NOT dispatch. A workflow_dispatch run resolves refs/heads/<branch>, so it tests the branch, not the merge result: on a conflicted PR that is a green signal for a tree that will never exist. The workaround in step 3 is for a MERGEABLE PR whose run never fired. | Read the PR’s head_sha. | mcp__github__actions_list → list_workflow_runs, filtered by branch, and find a run whose head_sha matches. | No run for that sha → the branch is NOT ready, whatever the PR page shows. Say so in those words rather than “checks pending”, and re-run them with mcp__github__actions_run_trigger → run_workflow against the branch. | Re-check after every push. A new commit moves the head, and the head is what the absence attaches to. | . An agent holding a standing merge authorisation must not read zero checks as nothing-red: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean, at the merge decision as everywhere else. | One branch. Develop on the assigned claude/* branch; moving work to a different branch needs explicit permission. | NEVER DELETE A FEATURE OR branches/ BRANCH without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Not after a merge, not as cleanup, not to quiet a tool that complains about it, and never by passing --delete-branch or its API equivalent. A merged branch is still the record of how the work was done, the base a revert or a follow-up is cut from, and the ref a staging deploy is served under. Deleting it is irreversible from the agent’s side and buys nothing the owner asked for. The same rule is in prepare-merge-auto.md Phase 4 and the anti-patterns, because an agent following either skill must meet it. If you change one copy, change the other. When a tool or hook complains about a branch, fix the tool — for example a reachability check in a stop hook — never delete the branch. | .

1488.title: Publish verification, and the one alert
1488.content: Skill publish-verification: Verify what a publish produced, and alert the publication manager whenever any step after the publish button fails — the verifier set, how to add a verifier, what is in scope, and how the publication manager triages the one alert. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . The verifier set runs over the built site before it is deployed. It does not stop the deploy: its outcome is judged after the push, and any failure reaches the publication manager through the same single alert as every other step after the publish button.

1489.title: The two processes
1489.content: . | publish-verification.bpmn — the verifier set over the built tree, between the export and the deploy. Pass, fail, or could-not-tell; the caller deploys either way and judges the outcome after the push. | publish-alert.bpmn — ONE alert, called from every failure edge in docs-site-publish.bpmn: a refused security gate, a failed deploy, a lost preview, a failed built-site check. It reaches the role that already owns the release: the publication manager. | .

1490.title: The verifier set
1490.content: bun run cat publish:verify -- --dir <built site> [--report out.md] — scripts/publish-verify.ts. Exit 0 pass · 1 a finding · 2 could not tell. The caller treats 1 and 2 alike: an unverified release is not a verified one. Each verifier is one entry in VERIFIERS: an id, the question it asks, and a function from the directory to findings. Adding a verifier is adding an entry; the report, the exit code and the alert need no change. Give it a test that builds a document to break it, as publish-verify.test.ts does. jsonld-expand is the first: every JSON-LD document of ours is expanded by a real processor (jsonld.js, network refused). A key the @context does not declare is DROPPED by a processor, silently.

1491.title: A verifier the preview cannot ask is a release failure waiting (STRICT)
1491.content: The staging preview runs the same verifier set, so a preview is never greener than the release it previews. That promise breaks wherever the preview answers a different question. It serves the PUBLISHED search index (--search-index borrowed), so search-index there asks only “present and parsing”, never “does it cover the pages” — so a preview can be green while the release refuses it. So the preview asks the coverage question of the index it built, before swapping in the published one: publish-verify.ts --dir ./_site --only search-index. The rule, for any verifier added later: if the preview substitutes an input, the verifier runs on the preview’s own input before the substitution. A check only the release asks fails after merge, on main, where everyone pays for it. Deliberate exclusion is marked in what is built. search_exclude: true is front matter, and front matter is gone after Jekyll. head_custom.html writes <meta name="fa-search-exclude"> for it, and search-index leaves those pages out of the coverage denominator and COUNTS them in its finding. An exclusion the built page does not carry cannot be told from a truncated index, and the release check will refuse it, correctly.

1492.title: What is in scope
1492.content: A document is ours when its @context names our content context or binds a namespace in the own-namespaces code list. Everything else in the tree — an ingested IG’s artefact index, for example — is counted as out of scope, reported, and never able to block the release.

1493.title: Triage, for the publication manager
1493.content: The alert is a tracking issue labelled publication-manager: opened on the first failure, commented on for each later one (a comment notifies; an edit does not), closed by the next clean publish. The issue says which step failed and whether the site deployed: . | Nothing was deployed (the export, or verification) — the live site is the previous publish. Hold, or fix forward. | The site deployed and something after it failed (a lost preview) — it is live. Say so in the issue before fixing. | . The label names the role, not a person: no actor declares a GitHub account for publication-manager. Watching the label is how a person takes the role.

1495.title: QA report signing — two routes, chosen by the performer’s reach
1495.content: Named by: Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A QA report becomes evidence when a third party can establish what was measured and who vouches for it. folio-test-run/v1 (schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts) answers the first: a data hash and a process hash, each all-or-nothing, plus the skill it tests, whose contract its recorded cases are checked against (test-run-conforms). This skill answers the second, and it has two routes because the participant doing the signing may not be able to reach anything: some machine actors are air-gapped, an API cannot be called from one, and a human actor signs instead. The subject signed is the QA report. This skill builds on signing. That skill holds what is true of any signature: who signs, what is signed, which suites a trust anchor accepts, key custody, the route, and what a verifier must check and record. This one keeps only what is particular to QA reports: the run hashes, the qa-reports branch, and the line between attestation and certification. Where the two overlap, signing is the rule.

1496.title: The process is executable — do not hand-roll the branch
1496.content: sdlc/processes/qa-report-signing.bpmn, with the branch computed by decisions/signing-route.dmn. Run it with workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete like every other diagram here. The gateway refuses a hand-supplied outcome: the route is a consequence of declared facts, not a preference.

1497.title: Reach is a property of the ACTOR, and unknown is a third state
1497.content: schemas/process/actor-reach.ts. | One vocabulary, two levels. An actor’s reach uses the same scale as the deployment’s network — internet, egress-restricted, air-gapped. There is no second scale, because two spellings of one fact drift apart. | Composition is asymmetric. An air-gapped deployment forces every actor air-gapped. A connected one forces nothing — a connected site may hold an isolated signing host. So an actor that declares no reach inside a connected deployment is unknown, not internet. | unknown routes to the human. A gateway that read could-not-determine as “use the API” would fail closed on the wire and open in the record: the call fails and what survives is an unsigned report that nothing marks as unsigned. Could-not-check is never green. | .

1498.title: Reach is declared, not a capability
1498.content: There is no network-egress capability. A capability is an environment probe — detection: { method: "command", … }, a thing you run to find out. Reach is an architectural fact, declared by whoever built the site. On an air-gapped host a failed probe is indistinguishable from an outage, and the safe reading of an outage (“retry later”) is the unsafe reading of an air gap. A capability would also carry the same fact as reach in a second place, free to disagree. What is a probe is whether an endpoint is configured: signing-api, an env-var detection. The DMN table reads both, because they answer different questions — can this host call out and is there anything to call. A configured endpoint on an air-gapped host is still uncallable.

1499.title: Declaration and execution are different mechanisms
1499.content: qa-report-signing.ts declares: . requiredCapabilities: [ { capabilityId: "signing-api", degradation: "fallback", fallbackRole: "publication-manager" }, ], . fallbackRole says which lane takes over when no capability can do it. It does not route anything, and nothing executes it; the gateway is what executes. They must agree — the declaration is what a reader and check:fallback-roles can see without executing anything; the gateway is what happens. Where they disagree, the diagram is what ran, and the declaration is the bug.

1500.title: Recording the attestation
1500.content: Record what signing §6 requires (suite, key, anchor, result, when checked) and, above all, which route signed it, not only that it is signed. The two are not interchangeable: one attests that a service with a key saw these hashes, the other that a person holding release authority did.

1501.title: Where the signed report goes: the qa-reports branch, next to its run
1501.content: A QA report is a derived record — it can be rebuilt from the tree and the data it hashed — so it is kept where every derived QA result is kept: the orphan qa-reports branch, in the entry keyed by the commit it judged (main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/), written through scripts/qa-store.ts and never by a hand git push. The signature and the route that produced it travel with the report, in the same entry, because a signature separated from the bytes it covers attests nothing a reader can check. Task_RecordAttestation in qa-report-signing.bpmn ends there. What does not go there. A certification — an accountable role’s Decision taken on a test report’s rollup — is a separate node, and it stays on main beside the attestations: it is a judgement, the same class as test/attestations/, and no regeneration can reproduce it. That decision belongs to the test-plan process, which calls this one to sign; this skill only signs. A read of a signed report follows the store’s rules: a miss is never read as “unsigned and fine”, and a store that cannot answer is UNKNOWN, which routes like unknown reach — to a person, never to a pass.

1503.title: QA reports — derived results on a branch, judgements on main
1503.content: Skill qa-reports: Where a QA result lives now. Derived verdicts go to the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by commit, written by the CI job qa-publish. Judgements stay on main in the attestations graph. Gates compute and judge against a stored baseline, and a missing one is unknown. Read before you regenerate, commit, resolve, cite or delete anything under test/results/ or test/attestations/. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A QA result is either reproducible or it is not, and that decides where it lives. A script verdict is a pure function of the tree: run the producer again and you get it back. A reviewer’s judgement is not, because no re-run can reproduce what an agent or a person decided. The two are split on that line: . |   | derived | judgement | . | what | every reviewer.kind: script entry: kg-qa/**, *.qa-results.json, witnesses, lsi/, tool-runs/, the health report | agent, human and baseline-pair attestations (a baseline is a judgement) | . | graph typology | qa (and health) | attestations | . | written to | <instance>/test/results/**, the working copy | <instance>/test/attestations/<family>/<mirrored subject path>.attestations.json | . | record | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/ | main | . | schema | the family’s own | qa-attestations/v1, schemas/sdlc/qa-attestations.ts | . | on a merge conflict | take the base’s side (merge:main), then regenerate | a person reads both sides | . cat-harness and the content core do not commit the derived files. Where a layer still does, they are a copy on its way out, not the record. Do not regenerate one in order to commit it, and do not hand-resolve one. Every qa directory declares storage and is ignored by version control, so a new file there is not committed. Before a layer’s removal of its committed copy is pushed, bun run cat qa:verify-moved --key main/<head> must answer IDENTICAL. It compares every moved path’s blob id with the entry, and an entry it cannot read is UNKNOWN (exit 2), never a pass.

1504.title: The branch
1504.content: qa-reports (orphan; never merged; author folio-qa-bot) ├── index.json newest entry per ref ├── main/<commit-sha>/ one tree per main commit that published │ ├── manifest.json inputs, producers, the gates' result │ └── <instance>/test/results/** byte-identical to the checkout's layout └── pr/<number>/<head-sha>/… same shape, pruned 7 days after close . Everything goes through cat-harness-tools/scripts/qa-store.ts, and nothing else writes the branch. check:workflows fails a raw push (qa-reports-unretried). | command | does | . | bun run cat qa:fetch [--ref main\|<sha>\|pr/<n>] | read an entry | . | bun run cat qa:publish --ref main/<sha>\|pr/<n>/<sha> | write one. Fetch the tip, splice, commit-tree -p, push without -f, 3 attempts with backoff | . | bun run cat qa:refresh | produce the working copy a publish stores, and say whether it is complete (below) | . | bun run cat qa:publish --github --completeness <report> | CI’s form: derive the key, skip a fork PR with a ::notice, and refuse an incomplete refresh | . | bun run cat qa:prune [--apply] | retention, as a dry run unless --apply. Daily in qa-reports-prune.yml | . A read answers one of five states. hit exits 0, miss 1, usage 2, corrupt 3, unknown 4. A miss is never read as “no findings”. A reader must not turn an absent entry into an empty, clean directory. What qa-publish stores is produced in that job, not handed over by the gates. The gates are in judge mode and write nothing, so their checkout holds only what is committed. So qa:refresh runs first. While the checkout still tracks test/results/, it runs nothing, because the commit’s own copy is the record and main/<sha> must be byte-identical to it. Once nothing is tracked there, it runs every writer declared in QA_WRITERS (scripts/qa-refresh.ts) into the empty tree. Then it checks three things. A file no writer claims, a writer that produced nothing, or a writer that exited outside its declared exits makes the run INCOMPLETE: the job fails, and qa:publish --completeness refuses to store it. A partial entry is never published as the commit’s record. Adding a QA writer means adding it to QA_WRITERS, or the first CI run after its first file lands goes red naming the unclaimed path. qa-publish is a job, not a gate. It runs after gates whatever they concluded (the evidence of a red commit is evidence too). It is the only job holding contents: write, and bun run cat gates never runs it locally. Its red means the record was not stored, never that the commit is bad (ci-health). Diagram: sdlc/processes/qa-publish.bpmn, called from Task_QaPublish in code-quality-gates.bpmn. Whose branch: each layer publishes its own . The branch is the store of the repository that declares it. A layer repository that declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, keyed by commit) keeps its results on cat/cat-harness/qa-reports of its own repository, keyed by its own commits. Its .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calls the tools layer’s reusable layer-qa-publish.yml, which audits that one layer with the layer at the pushed commit and publishes main/<sha> or pr/<n>/<sha>. An index reads a mounted layer’s results from that layer’s store at the commit its lock pins (scripts/layer-qa.ts, readQaTreeAtCommit), and never from its own store. A pin the layer has not published is a miss naming the commit. cat-harness, and the layers it hosts (kgQaHomeFor “hosted”), are still written by the index’s qa-publish. A layer that stops committing test/results/ without a publisher keeps its verdicts nowhere, so setting a layer up includes the caller (initialization step 5, sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10 “its QA record”), and init-folio --instance writes it.

1505.title: Gates compute and judge
1505.content: A gate over the qa graph does not compare a fresh run against a committed file, because the committed file is not the record. Its --check form computes and judges, and writes nothing: . | A finding fails only if it is NEW against a baseline. The baseline is the committed working copy for now, and --against <ref> reads it from qa-reports (for example --against main). Inherited findings are counted and reported, but they do not fail this change. | A missing baseline is UNKNOWN. It is printed, it is never a pass, and it is never a fail, because an unwritten baseline is not this change’s defect. | The four judge states are ok (exit 0), finding (1), unknown (2) and error (2), from JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. An unknown from a source that would not read outranks a finding, because a sweep that was blind on one part has not cleared the others. | . Each script’s docblock says which form it is in.

1506.title: Attestations
1506.content: . | A writer moves judgements as it saves. If a writer finds judgements in a prior derived file and the store holds no entry for them, it moves them into the store as it saves. bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate does a whole layer at once, and :check exits 1 while any judgement is still only in a derived file. | A corrupt store reads UNKNOWN and is refused. No writer overwrites it, and no writer regenerates past it. | Two disagreeing judgements are a person’s to reconcile. The migration refuses that case, and so should you. Never take one side. | Commit the store file. It is authored content on main, the same class as a review verdict. | .

1507.title: What to do, by situation
1507.content: | you are about to | do instead | . | regenerate a test/results file and commit it | regenerate it so the gates see the tree; qa-publish stores the record | . | resolve a conflict in test/results/ | bun run cat merge:main takes the base’s side, then bun run cat regen (prepare-merge) | . | resolve a conflict in test/attestations/ | read both sides. Keep both judgements unless they are the same one | . | cite a derived result | qa-reports:main/<sha>/<path> (decision-audit) | . | read a result in a test | build a fixture, or read it through readQa and assert the state (test-engineer) | . | delete a result to clear a sweep | don’t (deletion-requires-confirmation) | .

Every qa directory sets it, and each working copy is ignored by version control. | content-context-and-state-graphs explains why both halves are state, and why only one of them can be rebuilt. | qa-witness covers the published projection of a verdict. | .

1510.title: Release epic planning
1510.content: Skill release-epic-planning: Plan and track releases using work item epics. Covers epic creation, story/task decomposition, release readiness tracking, and the relationship between epics and GitHub milestones. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load . A release epic groups all the work for a specific release version. This skill governs how to create, structure, and track them.

1511.title: Epic structure
1511.content: The work items hierarchy for a release: . epic: "Release v0.2.0" ├── feature: "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" │ ├── task: "Add Phase 4b to crdm-requirements-workflow.md" │ └── task: "Update phase table" ├── feature: "Release lifecycle skills" │ ├── task: "Create release-lifecycle.md" │ ├── task: "Create code-review-process.md" │ └── task: "Create branch-freshness.md" └── bug: "Fix 7 BPMN isMarkerVisible attributes" └── task: "Add isMarkerVisible to 5 files" . Bean types in a release context . | Type | Role in release | Granularity | . | epic | The release itself | 1 per release | . | feature | A capability area / user story | 1 per feature | . | task | A single PR-sized implementation unit | 1 per PR | . | bug | A defect fix included in the release | 1 per fix | . | milestone | A session-scoped work container | Not release-scoped | . Creating the hierarchy . # 1. Create the release epic beans create "Release v0.2.0" --type epic # 2. Create features under it beans create "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" --type feature beans update <feature-id> --parent <epic-id> # 3. Create tasks under features beans create "Add Phase 4b to workflow" --type task beans update <task-id> --parent <feature-id> . Always check before creating — beans create is not idempotent. See todo-manager.md §”Check before you create”.

1512.title: Ordering within a release
1512.content: Apply the Phase 4b formalize-first rule from crdm-requirements-workflow.md: . | Structural/organizational work first | Process/policy formalization second | Implementation third | Visualization/UI last | . Within the epic, number features by dependency order. The first feature completed should not depend on any later feature.

1513.title: Release readiness
1513.content: Tracking readiness . The work items visualizer (<base>/beans/) shows open work items grouped by epic. A release is ready when its epic shows 0 open work items. Readiness checklist . Before moving from draft to pre-release: . | All must-have features resolved (all child work items completed) | All should-have features either resolved or deferred to next release | CI green on main (bun run cat gates) | All changed BPMN diagrams re-rendered | All changed docs pages regenerated | Changelog written (see release-lifecycle.md) | BA has reviewed accumulated changes | . Deferring to next release . If a should-have or nice-to-have feature won’t make the release: . # Move the feature bean to the next release epic beans update <feature-id> --parent <next-epic-id> . Record the deferral reason in the work item body: . beans update <feature-id> --body-append "Deferred to v0.3.0: not blocking v0.2.0" .

1514.title: GitHub milestone integration (optional)
1514.content: A GitHub milestone can mirror the release epic for stakeholder visibility: . # Create milestone gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/milestones --method POST \ -f title="v0.2.0" -f description="Release v0.2.0" # Assign PRs to milestone gh pr edit <number> --milestone "v0.2.0" . The milestone’s completion percentage gives stakeholders a progress view without needing access to the work items store.

1515.title: Cross-domain applicability
1515.content: | Domain | Epic title | Features | . | Code | “Release v0.2.0” | Skills, schemas, pipeline changes | . | Paper | “Publication: Chapter 3 revision” | Section rewrites, figure updates | . | Project | “Deliverable: Phase 1 report” | Analysis sections, appendices | . The hierarchy and readiness tracking are identical.

1516.title: Rules
1516.content: . | One epic per release — if scope creeps, split the epic | Features are independently reviewable — each can be a PR | Tasks are PR-sized — one task, one PR, one review cycle | Never close an epic without BA approval — the epic is the release | Deferred features move to the next epic — they are not deleted | .

1520.title: Semver policy

Requires downstream folios to update. | Rename a block kind, remove a pipeline stage | . | Minor (0.X.0) | New backward-compatible capability. New skills, tools, block kinds, BPMN workflows. | Add a skill, add a docs page | . | Patch (0.0.X) | Bug fix, typo, documentation correction, CI fix. 1521.content: | Type | Gate | Who decides | . | Draft | First PR for a planned release merges | Agent creates, BA approves | . | Pre-release (RC) | All must-have work items resolved, the full suite green on the candidate (§”The release gate”) | BA decides when to test | . | Named release | Stakeholder sign-off on the RC | BA + stakeholders | .

1522.title: The release gate: the full suite runs for a release
1522.content: Owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08: “not all CI needs to run unless doing a release build”, “you can merge to main and not be release build”, “CI not gate on non-release merge to main”. So CI has three lanes, and only the last one gates: . | lane | what runs | gates? | where it shows | . | Pull request | the fast tier: types, lint, and the tests and gates the change can reach; no re-run of main | no: shown on the PR, advisory | a preview at branches/<slug>/, on request, and always for content PRs | . | main | the integration run: the full suite on main’s tip, batched (one run per repository per hour, not one per merge) | no: a red run files ONE fix issue naming the merges in its range | the staging root of the site, not the live root | . | Release | the full tier as an absolute gate: every test, every gate, derive:publish, e2e, the standalone measure, the index at released layer pins | yes: nothing publishes from a red release candidate | the live site, the registry, the GitHub release | . What makes a merge a release: the PR carries the release label (or merge:guard runs with --release). The guard’s check 5 then gates the merge on green owed CI, as it did for every merge before 2026-11-08. A release candidate is cut from main after that merge, and only a green candidate is published (package-release step 3). What does not change: content still needs the owner’s authorisation; committee content never merges; the WHO repositories are not changed without the owner; CodeQL keeps its schedule. Those are authorisation and security rules, not CI tiers. What it replaces: for non-release merges, main-green-first (card Q-CIB-1 B, 2026-11-08), the 2026-10-23 ruling that a layer PR merges only on a green index run, and “merge non-content when green” in the merge window rules. Rollout (phased, owner’s choice A): 1. these skills, the merge DMNs and merge:guard (check 5 advisory unless a release); 2. cat-harness-tools’ layer checks (PR fast tier, the hourly integration run, the release run); . | folio-assistant’s Code-quality gates, previews on request, the site’s staging root; 4. the other layers and the re-pin train. Until a phase lands, its workflows still run in full: they are simply no longer a merge gate. | .

1523.title: Release planning with epics

1524.title: Where code review sits
1524.content: Code review happens at the PR level (before merge to main). Release approval happens at the RC level (after many PRs merge). PR → code review → merge → accumulate in draft release ↓ draft → RC → stakeholder test → named release . See code-review-process for the review detail.
