1595.title: translations/ directory rules
1595.content: The translations/ directory contains only three file types: . | .pot — POT templates (extractable strings) | .po — PO translated strings | .ts — TranslationNode manifests (KG nodes) | . Do not put .md, .qa.json, or status.json files in translations/. Rendered output lives in docs/<locale>/; QA and status are properties of the TranslationNode manifest. A layer with no translations directory of its own is hosted. translationsHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts its templates in the extracting harness’s translations/<locale>/<stub>/ — cat-harness/translations/<locale>/bootstrap/processes/*.pot for bootstrap’s three diagrams — rather than inside the layer, which holds no translation machinery. The templates are extracted from the bootstrap the harness has pinned; when bootstrap is its own repository they stay here, since a template is the harness’s work over bootstrap’s text, not part of it (kg-separation §”The pair”).

1596.title: A layer that defines its own translator
1596.content: A layer built on this one may define its own translator actor and translation subsystem. Then the rule is load it; never vendor it: the subsystem is invoked from that layer’s checkout, not copied here, and that layer’s skills say how. This skill names no layer above it.

1597.title: IG Publisher i18n
1597.content: For FHIR IG folios, the IG Publisher’s own i18n system is used in parallel: . | i18n-default-lang in sushi-config.yaml — source language. | i18n-lang — target languages. | translation-sources — path to input/translations/{lang}/ containing per-resource .po files. | Run with -generation-off -validation-off flags for fast translation-only builds. | . The prose translation pipeline (this skill) and the FHIR resource translation pipeline (IG Publisher) are complementary and independent.

1598.title: Do not
1598.content: . | Do not manually add badge includes. docs-ui.js renders them automatically from front matter. The include it replaced is deleted, not deprecated — an include that still exists is one somebody adds back. | Do not publish a semantic-QA number a script cannot establish. A back-translation from this repo’s own PO map, or from a word-substitution table, scores the table rather than the translation — and a string with no back-translation at all scores 0 and reads as drift. If no independent back-translator has run, the criterion has no verdict, and saying so is the honest output. | Do not infer a locale from a directory name. docs/fr/index.md is French because it says lang: fr. A subtag match is wrong in both directions and neither failure announces itself — see The navbar filters by locale. | Do not add a graph typology for translated content. It is the same kind of thing as the page it translates, differing by a field the file declares. Translatability is a property of a FORMAT within a content type — schemas/library/translation-tools.ts and isTranslatable — not of a directory. | Do not leave a translated page in the static nav. nav_exclude: true is what keeps it out, and no amount of client-side work substitutes for it: the nav is built once, for every reader, before anybody has chosen a locale. | Do not put non-PO files in translations/. Only .pot, .po, and .ts manifests belong there. Rendered .md goes in docs/<locale>/. | Do not vendor SMART Base translation scripts. Load from checkout. | Do not translate math, labels, or code. Exclude in extraction. | Do not auto-sign-off. Official status requires a human. | Do not re-extract per locale. Templates are extracted once, merged to main in one source PR, and every locale starts from them. | Do not open a locale PR into the source branch, and do not push to a branch whose PR has merged. Each locale is its own PR to main. | Do not fix the source in a translation. Report it as one issue. | Do not edit a FHIR resource to translate it. Its terms go into the locale’s CodeSystem supplement. | Do not re-translate a term a lower layer fixes in the same subject area. Translate with the locale term base, and fix a violation where the term is fixed. A use in another subject area is enforced once an adjudicator rules it in sense; until then it is pending, not a violation. | Do not treat staleness as “wrong”. A stale translation is still useful; it just needs re-review. | Do not conflate FHIR resource translation with prose translation. They are different pipelines with different tooling. | Do not auto-remove staging previews. Require staging:cleanup label. | .

1599.title: Content-type-specific translation tools
1599.content: Each content type declares what formats it can translate and what scripts handle each format. The declaration belongs to the layer that OWNS the content type, under contentTranslations in its <instance>.json; schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects every present layer’s profiles and refuses a content type declared twice. A module or diagram path in a profile resolves from the declaring layer, then down its needs chain. The profiles: . | Content type | Formats | RTL | . | document | Markdown | ✅ | . | paper | Markdown + LaTeX | — | . | dak (WHO L2) | Markdown + PlantUML + SVG + ArchiMate + Excel + BPMN | ✅ | . | ig (WHO L3) | Markdown + FSH + FHIR JSON | ✅ | . The generic pipeline (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts) handles Markdown. Adapter-specific tools extend it with format-specific extractors. The Python originals from SMART Base live in scripts/translation/ and are referenced in the registry. RTL support . Arabic (and Hebrew, Farsi, Urdu) pages are detected at load time by docs-ui.js and get dir="rtl" on <html>. The CSS in docs-ui.css provides smooth 0.4s transitions for sidebar and content layout: . | Sidebar slides to the right side | Content flows RTL | Mermaid diagrams and badges stay LTR | BPMN diagrams need re-rendering with translated labels | . Staging review . When presenting translated content for review, use the staging-review skill to provide before/after URL comparison tables. See schemas/sdlc/staging.ts for the StagingComparison schema.

1602.title: Adopting an upstream version bump
1602.content: Skill upstream-version-adoption: Watch a pinned upstream dependency for a new release, and take a candidate version through impact analysis, an MVP build, review and a person’s adopt/hold/decline decision. Reusable per pin — the theme is the first tenant, not the only one. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

1603.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
1603.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

1604.title: 1 — Watch
1604.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

1605.title: 2 — Impact analysis
1605.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

1606.title: 3 — MVP
1606.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

1607.title: 4 — Review
1607.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

1608.title: 5 — Decide
1608.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

1609.title: Adding a tenant
1609.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

1610.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
1610.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

1612.title: /watch — background watcher with integration check
1612.content: Skill watch: Background-watch a branch (default origin/main) or a GitHub PR for new activity while you work, and on every event report whether to integrate / whether it conflicts with the current branch / whether it lets you simplify exposition / proofs / computations . Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

1613.title: Invocation
1613.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

1614.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
1614.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

1615.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
1615.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

1616.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
1616.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the layer declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

1617.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
1617.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

1618.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
1618.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

1619.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
1619.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

1620.title: 6.  Output style
1620.content: Follow interaction-modality: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .
